case_study_insert.main_stem: Thornbury Mill Bakery (TMB) is a partnership in the commercial baking sector, employing a workforce of 50. Founded in 2013 by Amara Okafor, the business supplies bread and pastries to local cafes and schools and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership. TMB plans to invest $540,000 in energy-efficient ovens and recyclable packaging, financed by a $300,000 bank loan and $240,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $180,000 a year, a variable cost of $4.20 a unit and a selling price of $9.20, and currently produces 72,000 units a year. TMB faces high ingredient waste and a rising rate of customer complaints about stale deliveries, which are damaging its reputation with schools.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q4 2025: The bakery produced 18,000 units last month with a waste rate of 4.6%, down from 6.1% a year earlier. Customer complaints about freshness fell from 33 to 14 per week. Average delivery time is 2.8 days. A survey of 400 customers found that 66% would pay up to $0.30 more for recyclable packaging, and 51% check packaging before buying. A training audit shows 14 of 50 staff have not completed oven-safety training; local college courses cost $700 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Thornbury Mill Bakery for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.5%, increasing loan interest for businesses. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $12.60 to $13.49 per hour from April 2026, raising bakery wage bills. (3) Flour and dairy input costs have climbed 11.2% year-on-year, while consumer spending on bakery products grew 1.9%.

questions.question_text: Explain two advantages for TMB of using retained profit rather than the bank loan to fund the new ovens.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Using $240,000 of retained profit costs TMB no interest or capital repayments, protecting cash flow while it already meets $180,000 of fixed costs a year. With the base interest rate at 4.5%, interest on a $300,000 bank loan would be an avoidable burden; internal funds let the whole $5.00 contribution on each loaf stay in the partnership to absorb the 11.2% rise in flour and dairy costs without raising the $9.20 selling price to cafes and schools.

Point 2: Retained profit needs no security, so the $540,000 energy-efficient ovens cannot be repossessed if demand from local cafes falls, and the partnership keeps full control of its expansion decisions. There are no lender covenants to restrict how Amara Okafor runs the bakery, which suits a hierarchical structure where the founder directs operations. Using existing reserves also avoids delaying the project while a loan is negotiated, so waste-reduction savings from the new ovens can begin sooner.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: Consider local newspaper advertising, in-store supermarket promotions, or social media campaigns. Which should TMB choose to promote its recyclable packaged bread? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Local newspaper advertising: A newspaper campaign reaches local cafes, schools and households cheaply and suits a regional bakery supplying a limited area. The message is passive and cannot show the recyclable packaging that 51% of customers check, and print response is hard to measure, so it may not lift the 72,000-unit volume quickly enough.

In-store supermarket promotions: Demonstrations and shelf displays in supermarkets put the bread directly in front of the 66% of 400 surveyed customers who would pay $0.30 more for recyclable packaging, and can drive immediate trial. The cost of stand space, staff time and discounted trays can be high for a 50-staff partnership, and coverage is limited to the stores that agree to host the promotion.

Social media campaigns: Low-cost targeted posts can show the packaging and the freshness story to local buyers, with measurable engagement and the ability to respond quickly to the 14 weekly freshness complaints. Results depend on platform reach among older customers, and online interest does not always convert into bakery purchases without a nearby outlet.

Recommendation: TMB should choose in-store supermarket promotions, backed by cheap social media posts. Promotions reach the exact buyers who value recyclable packaging at the point of sale and can reverse the freshness-complaint problem through direct contact. Newspaper advertising is rejected as passive and unable to demonstrate the $0.30 premium; social media alone is rejected as weak at converting to purchases for a locally supplied bakery, so combining it with in-store activity uses each channel's strength. With $240,000 of retained profit already spent on the ovens, keeping promotion proportionate to the $5.00 contribution per unit is sensible.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies promotional options with limited application to TMB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discusses advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of TMB with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Evaluates all three options in the context of TMB with a well-justified recommendation explaining why newspaper and social-only options are rejected.

questions.question_text: Explain two benefits for TMB of using job enrichment to reduce its ingredient waste and stale-delivery complaints.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Job enrichment gives the 50 staff greater responsibility for planning their own baking and delivery rounds, so they take ownership of the 4.6% waste rate and the 14 weekly freshness complaints. When bakers schedule production to actual orders rather than following a fixed routine, less bread goes stale and ingredient waste falls, protecting the $5.00 contribution on each unit and supporting the $540,000 oven investment.

Point 2: Enriched jobs with more variety and decision-making raise motivation and commitment, which suits the democratic leadership described in the case. Staff who control their rounds are more likely to check delivery times and communicate problems with cafes and schools, reducing complaints. Higher satisfaction also lowers the burden on the 14 staff still needing oven-safety training, because experienced workers take pride in coaching colleagues and the $700 college cost can be targeted more effectively within the workforce of 50. This also supports the 72,000-unit target and the $540,000 oven investment.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the local college for the 14 staff. Which should TMB choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Instruction at the ovens is directly relevant to TMB's own equipment, costs no course fees and keeps the 14 staff productive while they learn, protecting the 18,000 units made last month and the effort behind the fall to a 4.6% waste rate. Drawbacks are that trainer-bakers lose time, unsafe shortcuts can be copied, and there is no formal certificate if schools and cafes ask for food-safety records.

Off-the-job training: The local college course at $700 per employee delivers structured oven-safety skills and a recognised certificate for all 14 staff, costing $9,800 in total — affordable against the $540,000 investment. It removes 14 of 50 staff from production, however, cutting capacity when 72,000 units are needed, and the generic syllabus may not cover TMB's exact ovens, so on-site follow-up would still be needed.

Decision: TMB should choose on-the-job training for day-to-day oven operation, adding short college safety courses for supervisors. It is cheaper, equipment-specific and avoids losing output while waste and freshness complaints are live problems; full off-the-job training is rejected because releasing 14 staff and spending $9,800 would disrupt delivery rounds to cafes and schools, and formal certification can be added later without halting production.

Additional considerations: The 4.6% waste rate and the fall in freshness complaints from 33 to 14 a week suggest process discipline is improving, so taking 14 of 50 staff off the line could jeopardise deliveries. A compromise is short college safety sessions for the 14 staff spread across several weeks, costing $9,800 in total but keeping output near 72,000 units while certificates are earned.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to TMB.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both methods in the context of TMB.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both methods in the context of TMB with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and equipment relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how TMB's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.
questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 36,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $5.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety against 72,000-unit output; pricing and discount modelling against $180,000 fixed costs; loan feasibility for the $540,000 ovens; and unit cost of $6.70 with productivity of 1,440 units per worker, used to reduce the 4.6% waste rate.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method and 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $180,000 ÷ ($9.20 − $4.20) = $180,000 ÷ $5.00 = 36,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 36,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $9.20 − $4.20 = $5.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $5.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways TMB's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 36,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 72,000 units, a margin of safety of 36,000 units, to justify the $540,000 oven investment.
2. Contribution of $5.00 lets managers test a school or cafe discount: a $0.30 concession leaves $4.70 per unit, showing the extra volume needed to cover $180,000 fixed costs.
3. Fixed costs and contribution set the output required to service the $300,000 bank loan before further expansion.
4. Unit cost of $180,000 ÷ 72,000 + $4.20 = $6.70 and productivity of 72,000 ÷ 50 = 1,440 units per worker allow weekly benchmarking and help attack the 4.6% waste rate.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate TMB's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Which ratio provides the stronger evidence of improvement? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 30.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 34.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 18.0%
ROCE 2024 = 18.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings: In 2024 gross profit of $1,080,000 = revenue $3,600,000 − cost of sales $2,520,000; $1,080,000 ÷ $3,600,000 = 30.0%. In 2025 gross profit of $1,377,000 = revenue $4,050,000 − cost of sales $2,673,000; $1,377,000 ÷ $4,050,000 = 34.0%. Operating profit rose from $540,000 to $729,000; $540,000 ÷ $3,600,000 = 15.0% and $729,000 ÷ $4,050,000 = 18.0%. Capital employed moved from $3,000,000 to $3,645,000; $540,000 ÷ $3,000,000 = 18.0% and $729,000 ÷ $3,645,000 = 20.0%. Interest payable was $60,000 then $75,000.

Evaluation: All three measures improved, so TMB's profitability strengthened. Gross profitability rose from 30.0% to 34.0%, consistent with better control of flour and dairy costs as the 4.6% waste rate fell. The operating return on sales improved from 15.0% to 18.0%, showing the $180,000 fixed costs are being spread across more output of 72,000 units. Return on capital rose from 18.0% to 20.0% despite capital employed reaching $3,645,000 to fund the $540,000 ovens, so the new assets are earning their keep.

Stronger evidence: the profit margin, because it gained three percentage points directly from the given revenue and operating profit and is not distorted by the larger asset base that also affects the return on capital figure.

Conclusion: TMB's financial performance has improved on every measure. The operating return on sales is the clearest sign of efficiency; the residual caution is the $300,000 loan and rising interest payable, which still need to be met from the improved margins.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three ratios for both years with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years, detailed evaluation of revenue, cost and capital movements, and a justified conclusion naming the stronger evidence.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for TMB of adopting recyclable packaging for its bread range.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Recyclable packaging matches the 66% of 400 surveyed customers who would pay $0.30 more, helping TMB protect its $5.00 contribution per unit while flour and dairy input costs climb 11.2%. The 51% who check packaging before buying make the change a useful way to win and retain cafes and schools, supporting the $9.20 price and the $540,000 oven programme.

Disadvantage: Sustainable packaging usually costs more than standard wrappers, which would lift the $4.20 variable cost per unit and squeeze margins unless the whole $0.30 premium is passed on. If the new packaging fails to keep bread fresh, the 14 weekly freshness complaints could rise and the 4.6% waste rate worsen, adding cost just as the $300,000 loan must be serviced. With $240,000 of retained profit already used in the $540,000 oven project, protecting the $5.00 contribution matters for meeting that loan and keeping the $9.20 price competitive for schools and cafes.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid point identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation applied to the named business.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.5%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase and the 11.2% rise in flour and dairy input costs will affect TMB. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Base interest rate (3.75% to 4.5%): If TMB's $300,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the 0.75 percentage point rise adds 0.0075 × $300,000 = $2,250 a year. That is small beside $180,000 of fixed costs, and zero if the loan is fixed-rate. Higher rates may make future borrowing dearer, but the direct annual cost is modest and TMB can reduce it by fixing the rate.

Minimum wage (7.1%, to $13.49 from $12.60 per hour): With a workforce of 50 in baking and delivery, this feeds into wage bills and cannot be avoided. The insert gives no hours worked or individual pay rates, so an annual total cannot be honestly invented; the defensible test is productivity of 72,000 units ÷ 50 staff = 1,440 units per worker. If productivity holds, the rise is absorbable; if it slips, unit labour costs rise and the $5.00 contribution narrows.

Input cost inflation (11.2% flour and dairy): The insert does not decompose the $4.20 variable cost, so only a bound can be stated: if all of it rose 11.2%, that adds 11.2% × $4.20 = $0.47 per unit; across 72,000 units that is about $33,800 a year (72,000 × $0.47). The $0.30 recyclable-packaging premium recovers only part of this, while bakery spending grew just 1.9%.

Conclusion: The 11.2% input-cost rise has the greatest impact because it applies to every one of the 72,000 units and directly erodes the $5.00 contribution that supports the $540,000 investment. The interest effect is minor and fixable, and the wage rise can be offset if productivity holds, whereas input inflation hits unit economics with almost no pricing room.

mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two changes on TMB's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in the context of TMB with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact.
